items.title: An objective wrong answer forces again
items.body:
Line 76 computes `forced = input.correctness === false`, and line 77 replaces the rating with `again` when forced. The `again` case sets step 0 and `dueAt = addMinutes(at, REVIEW_AGAIN_DELAY_MINUTES)`, which is 10 minutes. The result reports `ratingWasForced: forced && input.rating !== 'again'`, which is true here because the client sent `good`.

- "good, as sent" is wrong: correctness is exactly what overrides the rating.
- "hard" is a real rating, but nothing maps a wrong answer to it.
- "Refused with 409" confuses this with the revision check in the route; the scheduler never refuses, it reschedules.

items.title: A retake on the same version is practice only
items.body:
`isPracticeOnly(previousAttemptsOnVersion)` returns true as soon as there was any earlier attempt on that assessment version, because submitting the first attempt revealed the answers. The guide spells out the consequences: a practice attempt grants no fresh placement evidence and never revokes an existing `placed_out`. Fresh evidence needs a newly authored alternate version.

- "placed_out is revoked" is the opposite of the stated rule.
- "The retake counts as fresh evidence, so the failed result replaces placed_out" fails twice: the answers are already known, so the retake is practice only, and a practice attempt never revokes placed_out.
- "Back to in_progress" mixes up placement with lesson status; placement never changes lesson progress.

items.title: Easy adds two steps, and the new step sets the interval
items.body:
In `scheduleReview`, the `easy` case sets `step = clampStep(currentStep + 2)`, so a card at step 2 arrives at step 4. The due date is `addDays(at, intervalDaysForStep(step))` with the NEW step. `intervalDaysForStep(4)` reads `REVIEW_INTERVAL_DAYS[3]`, which is 14. `at` is the server acceptance time.

- "Step 3, due 7 days" is what `good` would do: good adds one step, easy adds two.
- "Due 3 days, the old step decides" gets the lookup backwards; the guide stresses the interval belongs to the arrival step.
- "Step 5, due 30 days" would need step + 3; easy does not jump to the top, it is capped at 5 only when step + 2 exceeds it.

excerpts.quote: The step number is where the card **arrives**

items.title: Concept: the review ladder and how a rating moves a card
items.body:
A review card sits on a step ladder from 0 to 5, and each step has an interval. The intervals are a shared constant, `REVIEW_INTERVAL_DAYS` in `packages/contracts/src/domain.ts`, read by `intervalDaysForStep` in `packages/learning-core/src/review-scheduler.ts`.

Trace `scheduleReview` with pencil and paper. For each rating (again, hard, good, easy), write down how the step changes, what happens at the top and bottom of the ladder, and which step's interval is then looked up: work out the exact array index the code computes, because off-by-one choices matter here. Note which clock the due date is measured from. Then check whether the rating the client sends is always the rating that gets applied, or whether something about the answer can change it.

Finally read `orderDueQueue` and write down its sort keys in order, before you look at the tests. The guide's exercise 1 is a good first trace.

items.title: Reviewed cards first, then new ones
items.body:
`orderDueQueue` keeps only cards whose `dueAt` has passed. It then splits them: `overdue` are cards with `lastReviewedAt !== null`, `fresh` are cards never reviewed. Each group is sorted by due date (oldest first), with `cardId` breaking ties, and the result is `[...overdue, ...fresh]`. A (due yesterday) comes before C (due today), and B, never reviewed, comes last even though it fell due earliest.

- "One list by due date" ignores the split; that order would put B first.
- "Most recent first" reverses the sort; `byDue` subtracts so the oldest wins.
- "Never-reviewed first" swaps the two groups.

The visible batch is 20 with an explicit continue, and there is no daily cap.

items.title: A solution reveal is permanent for that revision
items.body:
`resolveAssistance` checks `history.solutionRevealed` first and returns `solution_viewed` when it is set. The history is built from `RevealEvent` rows for the same `(exerciseId, masteryRevision)`, and those rows are never deleted. Resetting the editor does not touch them, so the next-day pass is still solution-assisted and cannot count as independent evidence.

- "none, the reset clears the flag" is the exact loophole the rule closes.
- "hints" is only returned when a hint, and no solution, was revealed.
- "Not recorded" is wrong: the attempt is kept with its assistance level. The app never erases assisted attempts.

A new mastery revision of the exercise starts with a clean history.

excerpts.quote: which are never deleted, so resetting the editor cannot change it

items.title: Recall alone does not demonstrate a concept
items.body:
`demonstrated` needs BOTH `distinctIndependentItemIds.length >= 2` AND `applicationOrDebugPasses >= 1` (evidence.ts:162-164). Two clean passes on different items satisfy the first part. But `EXERCISE_COGNITIVE_LEVEL` maps `choice` to `recall`, so `isApplicationOrDebugging` is false for both, and the second part fails. The status falls through to `practicing`.

- "demonstrated" forgets the application-or-debugging rule.
- "retained" needs demonstrated first, plus two spaced reviews.
- "unseen" only applies when there are no attempts and no reviews at all; these passes are attempts.

items.title: Overdue only relabels a retained concept
items.body:
Look at the order of branches in `classifyConcept`. `overdue` is computed, but it is only used in the branch `demonstrated && retentionPair !== null`, where it picks `review_due` over `retained`. A concept that is demonstrated without a retention pair takes the next branch and is labelled `demonstrated`, overdue card or not. The guide states the same rule.

- "review_due for any overdue card" ignores that the check sits inside the retained branch.
- "practicing" would mean evidence was withdrawn; history is never deleted.
- "retained" needs the retention pair this concept does not have.

excerpts.quote: A concept that is only `demonstrated` stays `demonstrated` when a card is overdue.

items.title: Start here: the rules live in pure functions in learning-core
items.body:
devpractice is a single-owner learning app. This quest is about its learning rules: how a review card is scheduled, when a concept counts as demonstrated or retained, how placement tests qualify, and when XP is granted.

Every one of those rules is a pure function in `packages/learning-core/src`, with an injected clock. The API only loads rows from PostgreSQL and hands them over. That makes the rules easy to read: open the function next to the guide and check each claim yourself.

Read `docs/learning-algorithms.md` from top to bottom, keeping these files open: `review-scheduler.ts`, `evidence.ts`, `assistance.ts`, `placement.ts` and `xp.ts`, plus the constants in `packages/contracts/src/domain.ts`. Then read `docs/data-model.md` to see which tables hold the evidence. The guide says it plainly: these are product heuristics chosen to be legible, not measurements of learning.

excerpts.quote: Every rule in this document lives in `packages/learning-core/src` as a pure function with an injected clock

readMore.why: What the rules deliberately do not claim, and the gaps the authors know about.
Which tables store attempts, reveals, reviews and XP, and the invariants they protect.

items.title: A failed critical item blocks placement
items.body:
`gradePlacement` computes two conditions. `meetsScore` is `score >= rules.minimumCorrect`, and the default minimum is 4, so 4 of 5 passes. `meetsCritical` is true only when no item flagged `critical` was wrong, because `requireAllCritical` defaults to true. `qualified` is `meetsScore && meetsCritical`, so one wrong critical item means no qualification.

- "4 of 5 is the only rule" forgets the critical-item rule.
- "practiceOnly instead of placed_out" mixes in a different rule: practiceOnly is about repeat attempts on a version, not about scores.
- "All 5 required" is wrong: the minimum is 4.

items.title: The top of the ladder, and the unused sixth entry
items.body:
`good` computes `clampStep(currentStep + 1)`. `clampStep` caps at `REVIEW_MAX_STEP`, which is 5, so the card stays at step 5. `intervalDaysForStep(5)` uses index `Math.min(5, 5) - 1 = 4`, and `REVIEW_INTERVAL_DAYS[4]` is 30. The sixth element, also 30, is never read; the guide's exercise 3 shows that changing it to 60 changes no schedule.

- "Step 6, index 5" ignores the clamp.
- "Wraps around to step 0" is what `again` does, not `good`.
- "Doubles to 60" has no basis in the code: the interval is a table lookup, not a multiplier.

items.title: XP measures activity, not mastery
items.body:
`exercisePassAward` returns `amount: XP.exerciseFirstPass`, which is 10, under the key `exercise:${exerciseId}:r${masteryRevision}`. Nothing in it looks at assistance: the guide says the award is granted whether or not the attempt was assisted, because the assistance is already recorded and shown next to the XP. Punishing it twice would add nothing.

- "None for solution_viewed" is wrong: no XP rule reads assistance.
- "5 XP, half" invents a rule; the amount is a fixed constant.
- "20 XP" is `lessonFirstCompletion`, a different award.

The unique `(userId, awardKey)` constraint makes sure the 10 XP is granted only once per exercise revision.

excerpts.quote: The first-pass award is granted **whether or not** the attempt was assisted

items.title: Concept: four records that must not be conflated
items.body:
The app keeps four kinds of record apart because they answer different questions. Lesson status says whether you worked through a lesson. Exercise evidence says what happened on one attempt and how much help you had. Concept status says whether an idea has been shown, and kept. Placement says whether you skipped a chapter by passing a test.

Concept status is special: it is never stored. `classifyConcept` derives it from attempts and reviews every time progress is requested, so there is no second copy that could drift from the evidence. Each attempt also records its grading origin (server, browser or self-reported) and its assistance level (none, hints or solution viewed). Those two fields decide what counts later.

While reading, keep asking: which record is this rule reading, and which does it write?

excerpts.quote: Opening a chapter, skipping a lesson, and passing a placement assessment are three different events. None of them is mastery.

items.title: Retention needs a seven-day gap
items.body:
`findRetentionPair` keeps reviews that were due, correct and graded `server_objective`, then looks for a pair on separate UTC dates where `second - first >= RETENTION_MIN_DAYS_BETWEEN_REVIEWS * MS_PER_DAY`. The constant is 7. Reviews 6 days apart are on separate dates but not far enough apart, so no pair is found and the concept stays `demonstrated`.

- "retained" forgets the 7-day rule.
- "review_due" is a label for a RETAINED concept with an overdue card; there is no early-review penalty.
- "practicing again" is wrong: evidence is never discarded, and the demonstrated passes still stand.

items.title: A read-then-update revision check can race
items.body:
The review route reads `reviewState`, compares `state.revision !== body.expectedRevision`, then calls `tx.reviewState.update` with a `where` of only `(userId, cardId)`. At READ COMMITTED, two simultaneous requests both read the old revision and both pass. The second update waits for the first one's row lock, then applies on top: the schedule advances twice.

- "409, as the A05 test proves" is wrong: A05 sends its requests one after the other, so it proves stale rejection, not this race.
- "Replays the first result" needs the same `clientEventId`; these differ.
- "SERIALIZABLE aborts both" is wrong: the transaction runs at the default READ COMMITTED.

The notes route shows the fix: a conditional `updateMany` that includes `revision` in the `where`.

excerpts.quote: where: { id, userId: owner.userId, deletedAt: null, revision: body.expectedRevision },
